extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and workshop participants
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules, games, and diagnostic exercises for ensemble improvisation: how to cooperate onstage, manage offers, build drama, structure short scenes (Master/Servant, Standing Wave, confessions), and diagnose common mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use genre conventions to liberate performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Start exercises or scenes in a clearly signaled genre (western, bank robbery, Jane Austen, Shakespeare) so improvisers know what physicality, tone and limits to adopt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genres impose automatic dramatic expectations and free players to commit (e.g., cowboy accents and big physicality for a western; subtle movement and restrained feeling for Jane Austen). Pick genres that will inspire and be fun for the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Players should not insert strings of adjectives that merely delay the story (e.g., 'We see a huge, green, scaly, slimy, ugly...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often used by players who want minimal control; it serves to postpone action and is a variation on 'that's not good enough' objections. Encourage concise concrete offers instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't take too much control or hog turns
rubrics_metrics.description: Players who feel comforted by maximal control may say extra words, mangled grammar or two/three words to dominate the key word or moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stop-and-apologize behaviors do more damage than a small extra word; teach players to commit succinctly and not to pre-empt partners' opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid peculiar pauses and hesitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Long silences before contributing filler words (e.g., waiting many seconds to say 'then') reveal a player who cannot commit without preconstructing the rest of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wastes time and is unhelpful in ensemble play; encourage instantaneous small offers and trust that partners will alter the unfolding sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist pointless originality that blocks collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid inserting odd, deliberately 'original' words (e.g., 'octopus') to appear clever when it resists collaborators and breaks discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a player thinks they can shine without others' input they should pursue less collaborative forms; in ensemble work, prioritize discoverable responses over showy originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use one-word/word-at-a-time games as diagnostic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Word-at-a-time and similar proto-story games ruthlessly expose technique and approach weaknesses because they run on pure instinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These games reveal who can commit, who uses shtick to paper over gaps, and are excellent for diagnosis of both player and coach. They are also audience favorites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be good to work with — enter to help, not to show off
rubrics_metrics.description: In ensemble exercises (like Standing Wave) players should enter to assist, rescue, or simply join, rather than waiting for a 'good' idea or trying to steal glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage players to step in because the time is right or someone looks uncertain. If nobody enters, prompt with 'Switch!' or point to someone. Better players know when to leave a scene well alone and when to jump in to rescue.

rubrics_metrics.name: In Standing Wave, substitute often and react to what's there
rubrics_metrics.description: When playing Standing Wave, aim for substitutions at a rate of about one every five or six seconds; enter quickly and react to the actual moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many people substitute at that rate, coherence is retained; nobody stays out longer than seven or eight seconds. Demonstrate if players struggle; small groups force participation and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When substituting, complete existing sentences accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Players who tap in must be able to accurately complete the sentence begun by the person they replace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to do so breaks flow. Demonstrate and rehearse accurate completions before repeating the exercise; practice in small groups if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't crash successful scenes to claim glory
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid entering scenes that are going well solely to 'share the glory'; conversely, don't stay offstage when scenes are stuck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a scene needs rescue; if it does, enter in a way that helps (e.g., simple physical rescue or a device that acknowledges the scene is bad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master/Servant status rules and addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: In Master/Servant exercises, Masters should play high status to the space (not necessarily to person), call Servants by first name, and Servants should address Masters as 'sir'/'ma'am' as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play initial roles in own sex; establish clear status through posture and modes of address to reinforce relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and focus rules in Master/Servant dubbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Masters adopt a gruffer/deeper voice and Servants a higher-pitched squeak when dubbing; Masters must look at the Servant and provide dialogue; Servants must pantomime lips and match expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masters who don't watch Servants can't supply fitting dialogue; Servants who refuse external dialogue undermine the illusion. Aim for bold pantomime without word-for-word synchronization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masters must respond quickly and not overthink
rubrics_metrics.description: Anxious Masters who think slowly need coaching; quick, unconscious responses serve the game better than conscious puzzle-solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate by playing Servant and making obvious offers; emphasize that the unconscious mind is quicker and audiences come to see that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servant's freedom and responsibility balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Servants can act unexpectedly (throw dinner in fire, etc.) and are ‘responsibility-free’ for initiating chaos, but must allow time for Masters to justify offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too many unrelated physical offers can collapse a scene. Teach Servants to give the Master time to react and justify before shifting to a new offer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jump-and-justify structure for confessions
rubrics_metrics.description: In Overconfessing exercises: (1) Servant 'jumps' by naming an item, (2) Master raises stakes and justifies importance, (3) Servant 'jumps' again to state the verb ('I [BLANK]ed them').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This order gives the audience information in the desired sequence: what was damaged, why it mattered, and what happened. It forces responsibility and encourages courageous, spontaneous offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master should raise stakes to justify Servant's fear
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Servant names something small (e.g., 'your handkerchief'), the Master should instantly amplify its importance so the Servant's panic makes sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use committed justification (even absurd details) to make the object precious. The Master's initial gasp and reaction convey importance; precise explanation can follow but commitment matters most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid waffle, blame-shifting and unnecessary repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Servants who waffle, hem-and-haw, or shift blame (e.g., 'It was the cook...') frustrate the audience; Masters who over-question or repeat info stall the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train pairs through iterations to reduce waffle. Teach Masters to know when they've had enough information; the audience cues when to move on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everything is an offer — listen even during long justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Long justifications or rambling speeches are still 'offers' that contain crucial information; players must listen rather than mentally prepare jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you mentally withdraw to plan a funny reply you will miss details that affect subsequent action (e.g., whether an object was a fighting bear or a teddy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding endings: reincorporate and vary closures
rubrics_metrics.description: After set iterations (e.g., three confessions), deliberately look for an ending; common endings include firing the Servant, death, lowered stakes, joining of protagonists, or reincorporation of earlier material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reincorporating the first thing gives a sense of full circle; endings can be sudden (e.g., mimed gunshot) or structural (lowering stakes). Use endings to teach scene-closure habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value emotional change: 'A changes B' as dramatic core
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic action is fundamentally when one character changes another (emotional reaction/alteration); scenes without character change feel like nothing happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize emotional reactions over plot mechanics. Encourage players to show internal change (ambition, guilt, humiliation) rather than only external events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise stakes by making characters care
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama and comedy rely on how much characters care: big reactions to big events (drama) or big reactions to small events (comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach improvisers to commit emotionally; avoid inventing ludicrous events with minimal reaction. Emotional investment makes changes meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage cooperative games to enforce ensemble habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use games that force cooperation (Arms Through, Speak In One Voice, Pillars, He Said She Said) to teach players to abandon control and work with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These games exploit cooperation and expose players who resist surrendering future control; they are useful for building ensemble skills other theatre forms may not provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace conflict—avoid scenes with too little trouble
rubrics_metrics.description: Too little conflict toward the middle of a scene makes it dull; conversely, too much conflict early removes the platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance conflict to create platform and rising stakes. Accept that getting characters into trouble (playing 'no' in story-appropriate ways) often yields discovery and audience pleasure.
